abstract: Goldman Sachs Research's first genuinely cross-country read on whether AI is visible in employment data, covering major developed and emerging markets rather than the US alone. Reported by CNBC on 2026-08-19; the underlying Goldman note was published the same week. The headline conclusion is deliberately narrow: AI-related hiring pressure is now clearly detectable in international employment data, but it is confined to a small set of industries and to workers at the start of their careers. The most quotable number is the call-center series, where US employment sits 39% below its historical trend, with Canada at 33% and Germany at 27% below. The paper matters for jobsdata.ai because it is the first source to put the US call-center and entry-level findings side by side with the same measurement applied to other rich countries, which is the natural test of whether the US pattern is about AI or about US-specific labor-market conditions. It also supplies an independent cross-national adoption benchmark built from eleven separate surveys.
keyFindings: Cross-country job openings: 'Industries with greater exposure to AI automation have generally seen slower job openings growth since the second half of 2022, with the relationship particularly pronounced in Germany, Australia and the U.S.'

Call centers are the standout: employment is 39% below trend in the US, 33% below in Canada and 27% below in Germany. Software publishing, management consulting and advertising have also 'fallen sharply below its historical trend across developed markets.'
Goldman reads this as causal-adjacent: the pattern 'indicates that AI-related employment pressures are already visible in industries where tools capable of automating work are available.'

Information and communication services employment 'has slowed across nearly all major developed economies since 2022' but 'remains near or above its long-run trend outside the U.S.' — the US is the outlier on level, not just direction.
Occupational analysis across more than 800 occupations finds AI headwinds 'strongest among entry-level workers,' plus a smaller additional negative effect for high-displacement-risk occupations.

Magnitudes: a 10% occupational AI exposure is associated with a 0.1pp drag on annual headcount growth economy-wide in France, Canada and the US. For entry-level workers the same 10% exposure implies more than 0.6pp (Australia) and over 0.2pp (US).

Adoption benchmark: Goldman combined 11 surveys measuring AI adoption across countries and put major developed markets at roughly 15-20% adoption, with France, the US, the Netherlands and the UK leading and Italy, Japan and New Zealand at the low end. Major emerging markets came in at 10-15%.
Overall verdict: 'AI-related hiring pressures are clearly visible in employment data globally, but remain limited to a relatively narrow set of industries and workers.'
methodology: Two linked empirical exercises inside a Goldman Sachs Research note. First, an industry-level analysis relating AI automation exposure to job-openings growth and to employment relative to a pre-2022 historical trend, run in parallel across major developed economies (US, Canada, Germany, Australia, France and others) so that country patterns can be compared under one specification. Second, an occupation-level regression of annual headcount growth on occupational AI exposure across more than 800 occupations, with entry-level workers separated out by seniority. Separately, Goldman pooled eleven existing national AI-adoption surveys onto a common basis to produce comparable country adoption rates. Effects are reported as semi-elasticities per 10% of occupational exposure and as percentage deviations from trend, not as counts of jobs lost. Accessed via CNBC's report; the primary Goldman note is not publicly posted.
qualifiers: Tier 2: sell-side research from a firm with a large commercial stake in the AI capex cycle, and accessed secondhand through CNBC rather than from the primary note, so the full specification, controls and standard errors are not inspectable. The below-trend employment measures are the weakest link — a trend break dated to 2022 will absorb post-pandemic demand normalization, offshoring, and the interest-rate-driven tech correction alongside any AI effect, and Goldman's own language ('indicates that pressures are visible') stops short of a causal claim. The call-center figure in particular predates most production-grade voice AI, so mechanism and timing are not fully aligned. None of the quantities map cleanly onto a jobsdata.ai chart unit: the 39%-below-trend figure is a headcount shortfall rather than the share of interactions automated; the 0.1pp and 0.2pp figures are per-unit-exposure elasticities with no exposure gap supplied to convert them to a level; and the 15-20% adoption band is a blended multi-country average with no US firm-level figure broken out against Census BTOS. All four therefore enter as overlays. The adoption band is still a useful external check: it brackets the 21.8% BTOS reading and places the US at the top of the developed-market range.
